questions.q: Why did Yahweh tell Samuel to stop mourning for Saul?
questions.a: Yahweh told him to stop because he had rejected Saul from being king over Israel.

questions.q: What did Samuel fear would happen if Saul heard he was going to Bethlehem?
questions.a: He feared that Saul would kill him.

questions.q: How did Yahweh say that Samuel would know whom to anoint?
questions.a: Yahweh told Samuel that he would show him what to do and that Samuel should anoint the one Yahweh told him to anoint.

questions.q: How did the elders of Bethlehem act when Samuel arrived?
questions.a: They came trembling to meet him and asked if his coming was in peace.

questions.q: What did Samuel think when he looked at Eliab?
questions.a: He thought that surely Yahweh’s anointed one was standing before him.

questions.q: How did Yahweh explain that he does not see as a human sees?
questions.a: Yahweh said that a human looks on the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks on the heart.

questions.q: What did Samuel say to Jesse after seven of his sons passed before him?
questions.a: Samuel said that Yahweh had not chosen any of them.

questions.q: Where was Jesse’s youngest son before Samuel called for him?
questions.a: The youngest son was out in the pasture tending the flock of sheep.

questions.q: What happened to David after Samuel anointed him?
questions.a: The Spirit of Yahweh rushed upon David from that day forward.

questions.q: What spirit troubled Saul after the Spirit of Yahweh had turned away from him?
questions.a: A bad spirit from Yahweh terrified him.

questions.q: What did Saul’s servants suggest a skillful player on the lyre could do for him?
questions.a: When the bad spirit was on Saul, the person would play the lyre, and would calm down.

questions.q: Which of Jesse’s sons did Saul ask to have sent to him?
questions.a: Saul asked Jesse to send his son David, who was with the flock.

questions.q: What assignment did Saul give David because he loved him greatly?
What would happen to Saul when David played the lyre?
questions.a: The bad spirit would turn away from Saul, and he would calm down and feel better.

commentary.text: Samuel sent to Bethlehem to Jesse.
Saul troubled with an evil spirit, is quieted by David.

Verses 1–5 It appears that Saul was grown very wicked. Of what would he not be guilty, who durst think to kill Samuel? The elders of Bethlehem trembled at Samuel's coming. It becomes us to stand in awe of God's messengers, and to tremble at his word. His answer was, I come peaceably, for I come to sacrifice. When our Lord Jesus came into the world, though men had reason to fear that his errand was to condemn the world, yet he gave full assurance that he came peaceably, for he came to sacrifice, and he brought his offering with him; A body hast thou prepared me. Let us sanctify ourselves, and depend upon His sacrifice.

It was strange that Samuel, who had been so disappointed in Saul, whose countenance and stature recommended him, should judge of another man by that rule. We can tell how men look, but God can tell what they are. He judges of men by the heart. We often form a mistaken judgment of characters; but the Lord values only the faith, fear, and love, which are planted in the heart, beyond human discernment. And God does not favour our children according to our fond partiality, but often most honours and blesses those who have been least regarded. David at length was pitched upon. He was the youngest of the sons of Jesse; his name signifies Beloved; he was a type of God's beloved Son. It should seem, David was least set by of all the sons of Jesse. But the Spirit of the Lord came upon David from that day forward. His anointing was not an empty ceremony, a Divine power went with that instituted sign; he found himself advanced in wisdom and courage, with all the qualifications of a prince, though not advanced in his outward circumstances. This would satisfy him that his election was of God. The best evidence of our being predestinated to the kingdom of glory, is, our being sealed with the Spirit of promise, and experience of a work of grace in our hearts.

Saul is made a terror to himself. The Spirit of the Lord departed from him. If God and his grace do not rule us, sin and Satan will have possession of us. The devil, by the Divine permission, troubled and terrified Saul, by the corrupt humours of his body, and passions of his mind. He grew fretful, peevish, and discontented, and at times a madman. It is a pity that music, which may be serviceable to the good temper of the mind, should ever be abused, to support vanity and luxury, and made an occasion of drawing the heart from God and serious things. That is driving away the good Spirit, not the evil spirit. Music, diversions, company, or business, have for a time often been employed to quiet the wounded conscience; but nothing can effect a real cure but the blood of Christ, applied in faith, and the sanctifying Spirit sealing the pardon, by his holy comforts. All other plans to dispel religious melancholy are sure to add to distress, either in this world or the next.
